demographics.trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another

Memory.value: I remember the frightening event as a few moments, and each moment is a picture in my mind.
When I remember the event I feel intense rage
Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning

Negative Appraisals.value: Nothing in my life feels meaningful anymore
I acted in ways that go against who I am
The event happened because of the way I acted

issues.item: Memory Feels Alien: The memory feels like it belongs to someone else rather than to me
issues.explanation: The trauma type is accidentally causing serious injury to another person. 'Memory Feels Alien' can occur in PTSD, but paired with the available appraisal pattern it suggests stronger dissociation/self-detachment than is otherwise represented; more importantly, the memory cluster centers on fragmented visual recall and rage, whereas the appraisal cluster centers on guilt/meaning plus personal bodily damage, making the profile feel pulled between different trauma experiences.

issues.item: Physical Vulnerability: My body has been permanently damaged by what happened
issues.explanation: 'Physical Vulnerability: My body has been permanently damaged by what happened' is hard to reconcile with the indexed trauma type, which is causing serious injury to another person rather than being physically injured oneself. Unless the event also seriously injured the patient, this item is clinically implausible. It also does not fit well with the Memory → Negative Appraisals formulation, because the memory items provided more naturally support guilt, shame, or moral injury appraisals such as 'Violated Values' rather than permanent bodily damage.

vignette:
Ramesh Patel is a 52-year-old South Asian American man who works as a maid in a downtown hotel, cleaning guest rooms on the early shift. He traces the change in his life back to one afternoon nine months ago, when he was helping his downstairs neighbor carry groceries into the apartment building where they both lived. He had been impatient and distracted, trying to get back upstairs before leaving for work. When the neighbor paused near the top of the exterior concrete steps, Ramesh moved around him with an armful of bags and bumped hard against his shoulder. The man lost his balance and fell backward down the staircase, striking his head and breaking several bones. Ramesh still describes the event not as a continuous memory but as a handful of frozen images: the plastic grocery bag splitting, oranges scattering across the steps, the neighbor’s face changing in an instant from surprise to terror, and the final picture of his body twisted on the landing below. Those moments sit in his mind like separate photographs rather than a story.

In the weeks after the accident, he found that the memory could arrive without warning, complete and immediate. At work, the sight of white hotel towels tumbling from his cart could suddenly become, in his mind, those groceries spilling across concrete. The thud of a vacuum handle hitting the floor in a guest room could bring back the image of the man’s body at the bottom of the stairs before Ramesh had any chance to prepare himself. When this happened, he did not just feel frightened. He felt a surge of intense rage as he remembered it, anger that seemed to have nowhere to go and yet was unmistakably tied to the scene. Sometimes the rage was directed at himself for having rushed; sometimes it flared at the whole moment, at how one careless movement could destroy another person’s life.

As these abrupt, picture-like recollections kept breaking into ordinary moments, they hardened his view of what the accident meant about him. Each time the images returned, Ramesh was pulled back to the instant in which he had acted in a way that felt completely opposed to the kind of man he believed himself to be. He had always thought of himself as careful, helpful, and responsible, especially with neighbors and elders. Now, when those snapshots came back, he was certain the injury had happened because of the way he acted—his haste, his impatience, his decision to squeeze past instead of waiting. The memory did not feel distant or softened by time; it felt like repeated proof. He had come to believe that he had crossed a moral line and shown something ugly and selfish in himself. In his words, “I did this because I was that kind of person in that moment,” and he could not find a way to separate the act from his character.

Over the following months, that conclusion spread into the rest of his life. Cleaning rooms, changing linens, and lining up toiletries had once given him a sense of order and usefulness, but now the work felt hollow. He still completed his tasks thoroughly, yet he experienced them as empty motions. Nothing in his life felt meaningful anymore. His divorce had already left him somewhat isolated, and after the accident he withdrew further, speaking to coworkers only when necessary and no longer calling his sister as often in the evenings. The strongest shift was inward: he no longer trusted the version of himself he had relied on for decades. What frightened him most was not only that he had hurt someone, but that the memory kept showing him the same accusation in flashes, as if his mind were insisting he look again and again at evidence of his own failure.

He is seeking help now because the problem has not faded with time. Last week, while cleaning a stairwell landing at the hotel, a guest dropped a bag of fruit nearby, and the scene slammed back into him so vividly that he had to grip his cart to stay upright. The old rage surged up at once, followed by the familiar certainty that his life had lost whatever goodness or purpose it once had. Ramesh told the therapist that he is afraid he will carry these images and what they seem to say about him for the rest of his life. At the same time, a quieter hope has brought him in: that he might find some way to remember what happened without being condemned by it every time it returns.
